title: Building a rabbit Morant ark
subtitle: A moveable open-bottomed run for meat or wool rabbits on pasture.
excerpt: A Morant ark is a triangular-section moveable rabbit house with an open mesh floor, designed to sit on grass and be shifted daily to fresh pasture. The design comes from the work of Major G. W. S. Morant in the 1880s and remains the most practical way to raise meat or Angora rabbits on grass without fixed housing. Moving the ark daily supplies fresh grazing and leaves the droppings to fertilise the pasture.
sourceNotes: Major G.W.S. Morant, Rabbits for profit and pleasure (1888), Internet Archive. British Rabbit Council, Morant system housing guidelines (2022). Ashley English, Keeping Chickens (similar triangular ark design), Lark Books (2010). Various smallholder adaptation plans documented in Smallholder Magazine (2021-2023).

glossaryTerms.definition: A triangular-section moveable rabbit shelter with mesh sides and an open bottom, placed on grass and moved to fresh ground daily. Attributed to Major Morant who popularised the system in the UK in the late 19th century for efficient meat rabbit production.

A rigid wire panel made from wires welded at each crossing point. For rabbits, 16-gauge mesh with a maximum hole size of 25 mm is the recommended minimum to exclude predators and prevent escape of young rabbits.

projectSchedule.title: Cut and prepare timber
projectSchedule.body: Cut all framing timber to length. Prepare the roof ridge pole, wall plates, and end frames. Sand any rough cut edges.

projectSchedule.title: Assemble frame
projectSchedule.body: Build the two triangular end frames. Attach the ridge pole and wall plates. Square up the structure and check it sits level on flat ground.

projectSchedule.title: Fit mesh and nest box
projectSchedule.body: Staple welded wire mesh to the roof and sides. Fit a solid-sided nest box section at one end with a hinged lid. Attach handles or carrying poles.

content.text: A
Morant ark

is a self-contained triangular rabbit house that sits directly on the turf. The rabbit eats fresh grass through the mesh floor during the day and sleeps in a solid-sided nest section at one end. Moving the ark each day to a new strip of grass supplies variety, prevents pasture fouling build-up, and mimics natural grazing behaviour.
Dimensions

A Morant ark for two to three adult rabbits or a doe and her litter needs to be at least 2.4 m long and 1.2 m wide at the base. The ridge pole height is typically 600 to 700 mm, giving a 45-degree roof slope on each side. One third of the length (around 800 mm) should be the enclosed nest section with a solid timber or OSB panel roof and removable lid. The remaining two thirds is open mesh.
Materials
Pressure-treated 50 mm by 50 mm softwood for the framing.
16-gauge
welded wire mesh
with 25 mm holes for the sides and roof sections.
9 mm exterior-grade OSB for the nest box roof, end panels, and back wall of the nest section.
Roofing felt for the nest section roof.
50 mm staples (for a staple gun) and 50 mm wood screws.
A 25 mm dowel rod for the carrying handles or two D-ring handles per end.
Building the end frames

Cut four pieces of framing timber at 45-degree angles for the two sloping sides of each triangular end (two end frames needed). The base of each triangle is 1.2 m; the two sides meet at the ridge at 45 degrees.
Join each pair of sloping pieces at the top with a halving joint or a ridge bracket. Clamp and screw. Add a horizontal base rail at the bottom of each triangle if you want extra rigidity.
Fit a ridge pole of 2.4 m length between the two end frames, screwed at each end. Fit two wall plates along the base of each slope, connecting the two end frames at base level.
Fitting mesh and nest section
Staple welded wire mesh to the two triangular roof slopes over the open two-thirds of the ark length. Work from the ridge down, keeping the mesh taut and cutting neatly around the frame.
Close the nest section: fit OSB panels to the roof and back of the final third of the ark, and cover with roofing felt. Fit a hinged lid on the roof section for access.
Fit a small entrance hole of about 150 mm diameter in the mesh partition between the open section and the nest.
Attach handles at each end: a 25 mm dowel rod threaded through holes in the end frames gives a comfortable grip for daily moving.

attrs.cue: Rabbits digging out at the corners when the ark is on soft ground
attrs.cause: The open base and rabbit's instinct to tunnel
attrs.fix: Peg the base of the ark to the ground with U-shaped wire pegs at each corner. A simple 300 mm length of 4 mm wire bent to a U-shape and pushed through the base mesh and into the ground is enough.

attrs.cue: Ark too heavy to move easily each day
attrs.cause: Over-building with too much solid timber
attrs.fix: Lightweight arks use 38 mm by 38 mm timber rather than 50 mm by 50 mm. The structure is strong enough for two to three adult rabbits and reduces overall weight by 30 to 40%.
